vignette:
He is 37 years old, Middle Eastern, married, and has worked as a firefighter for most of his adult life. Before the stalking began, he describes himself as someone who was cautious in the ordinary ways that come with the job, but not someone who spent much time looking over his shoulder. He is used to danger in the sense of smoke, collapse, and sirens. What unsettles him is not the kind of threat he can name quickly and respond to with training, but the slow, private kind that followed him home.

The stalking begins in a way he first dismisses as coincidence. A woman he has encountered briefly and repeatedly in the neighborhood starts appearing near the fire station, then near the grocery store, then on the street outside his home. At first he tells himself it is chance, that the city is small in the ways that matter. When the messages start, the tone changes. They are vague at first, then increasingly personal, referencing his schedule, his family, the route he takes to work. He becomes aware of her presence in a way that makes every ordinary movement feel exposed. He stops parking in his usual place. He checks mirrors more often. He changes the time he leaves the house, then changes it again. He does not tell his wife everything at first because he is ashamed of how quickly the fear gets under his skin, and because, as he says, he is a firefighter and is supposed to be the one who handles emergencies, not the one whose hands shake when a message lights up his phone.

As the stalking continues, his world begins to narrow. He scans sidewalks before stepping outside. He notices cars parked too long and people who look away too quickly. He starts taking different routes to and from work, even when that means adding twenty minutes to a shift already stretched thin. At the station he remains competent and steady, the same man his crew depends on during calls, but he feels the effort of holding himself together. The adrenaline that once helped him function now leaves him keyed up long after it is needed. He cannot settle into sleep. He wakes with his heart racing, convinced for a moment that he has heard a sound outside the window or that someone is in the yard. On some nights he gets up and walks the house quietly, checking locks, peering into dark rooms, trying not to wake his wife. He says the silence at night feels less like rest than waiting.

He begins carrying his phone with him everywhere and keeping the battery charged obsessively. He saves screenshots of messages, then reviews them repeatedly as if the pattern might become clearer. He reports the stalking to authorities and to his department, but the process feels frustratingly slow and insufficient. Each time he believes there has been a pause, another message arrives or another sighting occurs, and the sense of being watched returns all at once. He becomes jumpy at unexpected noises. A car door slamming makes him flinch. He scans crowds without meaning to. In public, he positions himself so he can see entrances and exits, a habit that makes sense in his line of work but now feels less like preparedness and more like inability to relax. He has moments when he is sure he sees her across a parking lot or reflected in a window, and the possibility that it is not her does little to calm him.

At home he is more irritable and withdrawn. His wife notices that he is present physically but far away in his mind. He loses patience over small things, then feels guilty and apologetic. He tries not to burden her with the full weight of his fear, yet the strain shows in the way he sleeps, the way he startles, the way he continually checks doors and blinds. He feels angry at himself for not being able to push it aside. He says the worst part is the loss of trust in ordinary life: the mailbox, the commute, the familiar route to work, even the safe feeling of home have all become contaminated by anticipation. He still goes to work, still enters burning buildings when called, but he notices that certain alarms are harder to shake off now, because his body no longer knows when danger ends.

Over time, he becomes less interested in activities that once helped him decompress. He declines invitations, avoids being alone in public spaces, and limits outings with his wife unless he can predict exactly where they will park and how long they will stay. The fear is not constant in the same sharp way, but it sits just beneath the surface, ready to surge when the phone buzzes or when someone lingers too long near the house. In sessions, he speaks with the controlled cadence of someone accustomed to staying composed, yet the shame in his voice is clear when he admits how much the experience has changed him. He does not describe himself as broken, but he does describe himself as on guard in a way that feels endless, as if his life has been reorganized around the expectation that the next unwanted message, sighting, or knock might come at any time.
